questions.q: Name the enzyme that catalyzes the committed step of glycolysis and the allosteric activator that signals high energy demand in the cell.
questions.a: The committed step is catalyzed by phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1), which converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. Its major allosteric activator is AMP (or ADP), which accumulates when ATP is depleted, signaling low energy status. A wrong answer (e.g., naming hexokinase or pyruvate kinase) reveals confusion between the first irreversible step (hexokinase) and the committed step (PFK-1), or ignorance of energy-charge regulation.

questions.q: Explain why glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm rather than in the mitochondria, even in eukaryotic cells that possess mitochondria.
questions.a: Glycolysis is an ancient pathway that evolved before mitochondria existed; it occurs in the cytoplasm because all its enzymes are soluble cytosolic proteins. Mitochondria lack the enzyme machinery for glycolysis — they only receive pyruvate via a specific transporter. A student who says "because mitochondria are for aerobic respiration" shows a teleological misconception (confusing evolutionary history with current function) rather than understanding compartmentalization of enzyme systems.

questions.q: A plant cell is supplied with glucose labeled with ¹⁴C at carbon-1 (C-1). After one round of glycolysis, in which carbon position(s) of pyruvate will the label appear? Justify your answer.
questions.a: The label will appear at the carboxyl carbon (C-1) of pyruvate. In the aldolase step, fructose-1,6-bisphosphate splits into glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P) and dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP). The original C-1 of glucose becomes C-3 of G3P (which is the aldehyde carbon). Through triose phosphate isomerase, DHAP equilibrates with G3P, but the label from glucose C-1 ends up specifically at the aldehyde carbon of G3P. This carbon becomes the carboxyl carbon of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and finally the carboxyl carbon (C-1) of pyruvate. A wrong answer (e.g., methyl carbon) indicates failure to track carbon rearrangement at the aldolase and triose phosphate isomerase steps.

questions.q: Compare the ATP yield per glucose in glycolysis versus the complete aerobic respiration of glucose. What percentage of total ATP is produced directly in glycolysis (substrate-level only), and why is this proportion significant for cells without mitochondria?
questions.a: Glycolysis yields 2 ATP (substrate-level) per glucose. Complete aerobic respiration yields ~38 ATP (theoretical maximum), so glycolysis contributes only ~5% of total ATP directly. However, glycolysis is the ONLY ATP source for mature mammalian erythrocytes (no mitochondria) and for parasitic worms in anaerobic environments. A student who calculates 2/38 ≈ 5% but misses the physiological significance shows inability to connect quantitative biochemistry to cell-type-specific adaptations.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "In glycolysis, the conversion of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (1,3-BPG) to 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PG) produces ATP because 1,3-BPG is a high-energy compound." Is the reasoning complete? If not, what is missing?
questions.a: The reasoning is incomplete. While 1,3-BPG does have a high phosphoryl transfer potential (ΔG°' = -49.3 kJ/mol), ATP synthesis occurs because the enzyme phosphoglycerate kinase couples the exergonic hydrolysis of the acyl-phosphate bond in 1,3-BPG to the endergonic phosphorylation of ADP. The "high-energy bond" concept alone is insufficient — the enzyme's active site geometry and the near-equilibrium nature of the reaction (ΔG ≈ 0 in vivo) are essential. A student who accepts the statement as fully correct reveals a textbook-level oversimplification common in middle school but inadequate for Class 11.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using yeast to demonstrate that glycolysis can proceed anaerobically and produces CO₂. Specify the control, the measurable variable, and how you would confirm the CO₂ originates from glucose carbon (not bicarbonate buffer).
questions.a: Setup: Two test tubes with glucose solution + yeast suspension. Tube A: sealed with a one-way gas valve leading to lime water (Ca(OH)₂). Tube B (control): same but heat-killed yeast. Measure: time for lime water to turn milky (CO₂ detection). To confirm carbon source: use ¹⁴C-labeled glucose at C-3/C-4 (which becomes CO₂ in pyruvate decarboxylase step of fermentation) and detect ¹⁴CO₂ in the gas phase via scintillation counting. A poor design (e.g., no control, or assuming all CO₂ comes from glycolysis) shows inability to isolate variables and trace carbon fate — a key skill for board practicals.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Glycolysis is the universal, ten-step enzymatic pathway in the cytoplasm where one molecule of glucose (6C) is partially oxidized into two molecules of pyruvic acid (3C), with a net gain of 2 ATP (substrate-level ______) and 2 NADH + H⁺ per glucose molecule.
Fill in the blank: When you eat a roti or rice, the starch is digested to ______ which enters your blood.
What is Glycolysis? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Glycolysis is the universal, ten-step enzymatic pathway in the cytoplasm where one molecule of glucose (6C) is partially oxidized into two molecules of pyruvic acid (3C), with a net gain of 2 ATP (substrate-level phosphorylation) and 2 NADH + H⁺ per glucose molecule.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Start by recalling that glucose is a ______-carbon sugar.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Glycolysis?
questions.a: Students often believe that the 2 NADH produced in glycolysis directly yield 6 ATP (3 ATP each) in the electron transport chain, so they add 6 to the 2 substrate-level ATP and claim glycolysis gives 8 ATP.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can trace the carbon skeleton of glucose through all ten steps, identify the three regulatory enzymes (hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase), calculate the net ATP/NADH yield accounting for the investment phase, and predict the metabolic fate of pyruvate under aerobic vs anaerobic conditions in plant and animal cells.
